title: Graph isomorphism in polynomial time
formal: Does there exist one deterministic classical algorithm that, for every pair of finite simple undirected graphs G and H given by explicit adjacency matrices, decides whether G and H are isomorphic in time polynomial in the total input length?
definitions: Two graphs on equally many vertices are isomorphic if a bijection of their vertex sets preserves adjacency in both directions. The input contains the complete graph descriptions; unequal vertex counts are rejected immediately. The algorithm must be uniform, deterministic and correct on every graph pair, with no promise of bounded degree, rigidity, expansion, or random input. Polynomial time is measured in the binary input length, so the \(\Theta (n^{2})\) adjacency data may be read in full. The question concerns ordinary vertex-permutation isomorphism, not quantum isomorphism, graph canonization under a different output requirement, or isomorphism of groups or tensors. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove the proposition in the problem statement or prove its logical negation, using exactly the definitions, hypotheses and quantifier order stated here. The proof must cover the complete target.
why: Tests whether the central equivalence problem for finite combinatorial structures can be recognized in deterministic polynomial time after the quasipolynomial barrier was broken.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved problem at the intersection of algorithms, permutation groups and complexity theory, with a precise best-known general upper bound.

context_blocks.text: Graph isomorphism asks whether two finite graphs differ only by a relabelling of their vertices. A proposed relabelling is easy to verify, so the problem lies in NP, but ruling out all relabellings can be difficult for highly symmetric graphs.

Many special cases have polynomial-time algorithms, including bounded-degree graphs and several classes with strong structural restrictions. These results do not automatically combine into an algorithm for arbitrary graphs, whose automorphism groups can have a much richer structure.

Babai’s breakthrough gives a deterministic quasipolynomial-time algorithm, with running time \(\exp ((\log  n)^{O(1)})\), improving the earlier subexponential bound. Quasipolynomial time is still asymptotically larger than every fixed polynomial, so the final gap to P remains exactly the question on this card.

Graph canonization is closely related: producing a canonical labelled representative is at least as demanding as deciding isomorphism in many standard reductions, but a theorem about one output formulation must preserve the required runtime and uniformity before it answers the decision problem. Quantum graph-isomorphism relations and BQP algorithms likewise concern different computational problems.

No general polynomial-time algorithm or unconditional lower bound excluding one was found in the checked literature through 11 September 2026. The problem remains a clean benchmark for the boundary between efficiently verifiable symmetry and efficient recognition of symmetry.

The introductory discussion in Butti and Dalmau's 2021 paper also poses polynomial-time graph isomorphism. The reference places the general question in the context of fractional homomorphisms, Weisfeiler–Leman invariance and Sherali–Adams hierarchies; the saved passage does not select a separate conjecture about one hierarchy.
